Premise is engaging and the game is cheap, but it certainly is a no-buy for me.

The game loop goes like this:
[olist]
[*] You receive a contract from one of the many contract hubs in the game.
[*] After receiving it, you will have to hack a computer and gain access to it.
[*] Once you have access, you'll have to search through its folders in order to find information and more nearby computers to hack. You might also find some more new tools.
[*] After you are done, you have to delete the logs of your target computer and disconnect.
[*] If you are not done, hack any remaining computers you found on step 3 until you get the objective done.
[*] Get a new contract.
[/olist]

Hacking progress goes like this: remote computers have a different number of closed ports which you have to open with commands that you acquire as you progress. Each open port lowers the toughness of the target computer and, once it's low enough, you can use a magic command to hack it and gain access to its contents. There are a few extra things (proxies, firewalls, time limit and some per-mission modifications) but overall the process is tedious and revolves around repeating the same commands over and over.

Some other reviews mention that this game has some learning potential, which is wrong. The commands that you execute take no arguments and just show progress bars which go up at the same constant rate, forcing you to be glaring at your screen until they are done. Any resemblance to an actual UNIX command is just the fact that they are, indeed, executed on a terminal emulator.

The game got tedious after an hour. If you enjoy the loop, you might enjoy the game, but be advised that it is repetitive, almost non-interactive and a bit dull. The story is not engaging at all and just revolves around people asking you to hack things.

Quite a fun game, got it from a humble bundle but just recently managed to play it. Plays a bit like a puzzle (action puzzle?), which doesn't sound that exciting but the game does have a few tricks up its sleeve to get your blood pumping (Roller Mobster, I'm looking at you).
Don't be scared by the unix-like terminal and command lines, the game will provide you with hints and tips to make the most out of the tools you have at hand, but be wary, as others have said, this game won't hold your hand. Personally, I've found the game a bit on the easy side, but its expansion might hopefully provide for a fair bit of extra difficulty (and game time, the base game lasts about 9-12 hrs which isn't too bad for its price, but it definitely could be better). 
Some might find the gameplay repetitive (and the game quite short) and although I've ran into some bugs while playing, it was nothing gamebreaking. There is minimal replayability, involving a mission in the early game that offers two diverging paths, but no alternate endings.
Overall I do recommend Hacknet for being a hacking "sim" that aims more for the fun factor than for realism, thus while it might not be for everyone, it's still much more approachable by the unversed in digital security than the real deal. Especially if you get it for cheap, as I did.

I found Hacknet to be a refreshingly original experience. The first few missions of the game provide give you a chance to find your feet and familiarize yourself with the various tools at your disposal; a must considering the game is played largely through console commands. Once you've gotten the hang of things and mastered the basics you'll be feeling like a top-notch hacker, but by then the game will stop holding your hand and you'll have to rely on your own wits to overcome the challenges and objectives presented to you.

The game boasts an awesome soundtrack; fans of EDM and Retrowave will find themselves right at home here. The game is text-heavy which may be a turn off to some players, but those who aren't deterred will find a plethora of optional content that goes a long way to immerse you in the experience.

I have not finished the game yet, but other reviewers have indicated that the main story contains about ~10 hours of gameplay with the DLC Labyrinths adding another ~10 hours. Workshop support is available, and there are already a number of extensions released by the community that add longevity to the game.

All in all, this is one of my most satisfactory purchases on Steam. If hacking interests you even slightly, pick it up and give it a spin. You won't be disappointed.

So it's remake of uplink.  

A weird and fictional method of "hacking ports". A sadly arbitrary number next to each computer is the number of unlock commands you need to run.     He did away with the world-map and routing your connections through various hops.   (Which was kinda silly to start with, but... a countdown from 100 is likewise kinda silly.   Now the rate at which it decrements varies.)

I only got so far as csec looking for Bit again, so maybe the story really picks up....   eventually.  But MAN is it drap getting there.    


But it adds nothing to uplink.   I guess... "tab" maybe?  There are a couple of systems that are different from what was in uplink.  Not really deeper, but just different.   And it's LACKING a lot of details and features that uplink had.    No more robbing banks for fun and profit.     It adds random quotes from bash.org, but is lacking the sort of inside jokes that uplink had.   The only real easter egg I found was hanging onto that encrypted file and eventually decrypting it to find that it was fake all along.   Which is kinda funny. But... it was just that one egg.    And part of it feeling barren in this area is that you only ever see things related to the mision. No free-form open-endedness.   No public list of servers.  You can't log into Peter Jackson's server.    Oh, and all the mission plot points are ALREADY there from the start.    So you've got missions requiring decryptions tools that you only aquire later.  And the file a mission tells you to download is already there before the mission ever comes up.   tsk. 

Hey, he DID have you hack into the encryption company and steal the decryption tool. That was a nice way to introduce a toy.  And he added was some tools for modding.  ...but I'm not seeing anything interesting. Just more... "content".   Which is kinda dull in itself. 

I wouldn't recommend it since it's like 80% of a remake that didn't need to be made.     If this sort of thing interests you, go play uplink instead.  If you've played uplink, you've practically already played this game.

I absolutely loved Hacknet - mechanically, musically and story-wise. It was so immersive and great at telling its story, even though the story itself was fairly low-key compared to many other games. Once, when I got a bluescreen, I had a moment where I was just staring at the screen, going "oh shit shit shit I've messed it up now" until, a few seconds later, I remembered that it was "only" a game. And that rarely ever happens (to me, at least). I also found myself actually caring for the "protagonist" after just a few hours, even though I only knew Bits and pieces about them in the beginning.

So, kudos to the developer, who made a really, really great game that made me shed a tear or two at the end. It's one of my new favourite games, without doubt, and I would love to see more games like this one.

Regarding the DLC - it was an awesome addition!
